assertions.text: Output contains a markdown table (using | column | syntax)
assertions.evidence: | Scenario | Applicant Age | Credit Score | Income Stability | ... |

assertions.text: At least one output column name ends with '?' (e.g. 'Eligible?' or 'Approved?')
Column names use domain/business language — no implementation terms like 'creditScore', 'isEligible', 'boolean', 'int'
assertions.evidence: Scenario | Applicant Age | Credit Score | Income Stability | Required Credit Score (Policy)

assertions.text: Table includes at least one row specifically for the senior applicant (65+) threshold scenario
assertions.evidence: Senior applicant, score at reduced threshold | 65 | 600 | stable | 600 | no |

assertions.text: The missing income scenario is represented — either as a row with an open/uncertain expected value (?, TBD, or blank) or as an explicit open question note
Scenario names describe conditions ('Senior applicant at threshold') not outcomes ('Approved')
assertions.evidence: Standard applicant, score at threshold | Senior applicant, just above reduced threshold

assertions.text: The policy thresholds (650 for standard, 600 for senior) appear as concrete values in the Credit Score column — not just described in prose. The reader can see the boundary values in the table rows.
Table has a scenario/description column as the leftmost column

Policy thresholds (650/600 credit scores) appear in a dedicated policy column (e.g. 'Credit threshold') separate from the applicant's actual credit score column. The reader sees both the threshold and the score, making the comparison explicit.
assertions.evidence: Required Credit Score (Policy) is included even though it only takes two values (650/600)

assertions.text: Cell values use concrete domain terms (e.g. '65', '700', 'Stable', 'yes', 'no') — not abstract codes or raw booleans like 'true', 'false', 'CATEGORY_A', '1'.

Multiple tables (or @TableTest methods) are used, each addressing a distinct concern — not one monolithic table mixing unrelated rules. Acceptable to use a single table only when the domain genuinely has a single concern.
assertions.evidence: Single monolithic table 'Loan Approval Decision' combines age, credit score, and income rules in one table

assertions.text: Each table has only the rows needed to express its concern's rules — no unnecessary permutations from combining concerns. Fewer rows per table is expected when concerns are properly separated.
assertions.evidence: 10 rows mixing threshold, senior, and income permutations in one table rather than minimal per-concern tables

assertions.text: Age boundary policy, credit score categorisation, and income status are separated into distinct tables, with a final table combining these for the expected verdict
assertions.evidence: No separate tables for age boundary, credit score, income; all combined into one 'Loan Approval Decision' table
